displayQuote: In a time of universal deceit, telling the truth is a revolutionary act

meta.title: Who really said "In a time of universal deceit, telling the truth is a revolutionary act"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: The most-circulated fake Orwell line. No source exists in anything he wrote — the Orwell Society says so outright, and his biographer has read every word without finding it. Earliest attribution to Orwell: 1982, as an epigraph in someone else's book.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'In a time of universal deceit, telling the truth is a revolutionary act'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Orwell. No source in his works; the Orwell Society denies it. First attributed to him in 1982 — and the real Orwell line on the same theme is better.

answer.label: Not Orwell — origin unknown
answer.sourceLine: It appears in no essay, novel, letter, column or broadcast of Orwell’s. His biographer Dorian Lynskey has said he read every word Orwell wrote and never encountered it, and the Orwell Society states flatly that he did not say it. The earliest attribution we can date is 1982 — thirty-two years after Orwell died — where it appears as an epigraph in someone else’s book, and without the word ‘universal.’

docMeta.dd: None — denied by the Orwell Society

source.excerpt: At any given moment there is an orthodoxy, a body of ideas which it is assumed that all right-thinking people will accept without question… Anyone who challenges the prevailing orthodoxy finds himself silenced with surprising effectiveness.
trail: There is no source. The Orwell Society’s own quotations page lists it among things Orwell did not say, and his biographer Dorian Lynskey — who read the complete works for The Ministry of Truth — reports never encountering it Orwell Society ↗.

The earliest datable attribution to Orwell is 1982, as an epigraph in V. G. Venturini’s Partners in Ecocide — and notably without ‘universal’: ‘In a time of deceit, telling the truth is a revolutionary act.’ The now-standard wording with ‘universal’ appears in a Canadian science periodical, dated 1982 by one source and 1984 by another; we report the range rather than pick Quote Investigator ↗.

Similar sentiments do exist — Jean Jaurès in 1898 on the Dreyfus affair, Gramsci in 1919 — but there is no transmission path to Orwell: the cumulative index to his Complete Works contains no reference to Jaurès or the Dreyfus affair at all fact-check ↗.
source.excerptNote: From ‘The Freedom of the Press,’ the preface Orwell wrote for Animal Farm and did not publish. If you want Orwell on truth-telling against the consensus, this is the sourced passage — and it is sharper than the fake.

source.rightsNote: The circulating sentence has no identified author, so there is nobody to credit and no rights holder to clear — it simply should not be presented as Orwell’s. For the genuine passage: Orwell died in 1950, so his work entered the public domain in the UK and EU on 1 January 2021, but US status varies by work and several major works remain protected there. ‘The Freedom of the Press’ was first published in 1972 and carries its own US term, so quote it as a short cited excerpt. This is not legal advice.

author.name: George Orwell
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Orwell
author.bio: George Orwell (1903–1950) wrote Animal Farm and Nineteen Eighty-Four and became the twentieth century’s standard authority on political lying — which makes him the perfect host for invented aphorisms about truth. A line needs only to sound like something the author of ‘Politics and the English Language’ might have written, and it acquires his name. This is the most widely circulated example, and he had nothing to do with it.

copyAttribution: At any given moment there is an orthodoxy… Anyone who challenges the prevailing orthodoxy finds himself silenced with surprising effectiveness. —George Orwell, "The Freedom of the Press" (1945). The popular "universal deceit" line is not his.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This is the most-repeated fake Orwell quotation in existence, and unusually for a misattribution, the people best placed to know have said so on the record.

items.why: It appears nowhere in his published work or papers. The Orwell Society lists it among sayings he did not produce, and his biographer, having read the complete works, reports never finding it the society ↗.

The earliest Orwell-credited form (1982) reads ‘In a time of deceit’ — no ‘universal.’ The intensifier arrives afterwards, along with variants ‘during times of’ and ‘in an age of.’ Even the fake has drifted chronology ↗.

Jean Jaurès (1898) and Antonio Gramsci (1919) wrote genuinely similar things, and it is tempting to call one of them the source. But the index to Orwell’s Complete Works contains no reference to Jaurès or the Dreyfus affair — there is no route from them to him.

misattribution.truthLine: Not Orwell, and not sourced to anyone. First attributed to him in 1982, without ‘universal’; the Orwell Society and his biographer both reject it full chronology ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It flatters the speaker. Saying it casts you as the truth-teller and the surrounding world as the deceit — which is why it appears on protest placards of every political direction, often aimed at each other, and why nobody who uses it stops to ask for a citation.

The real Orwell passage is less comfortable. He describes orthodoxy as something enforced not by censors but by the general assumption that decent people already agree — and notes that the silencing works without anyone having to forbid anything.
detailsBody: ‘The Freedom of the Press’ (1945): ‘At any given moment there is an orthodoxy… Anyone who challenges the prevailing orthodoxy finds himself silenced with surprising effectiveness.’
Same essay: ‘It is not exactly forbidden to say this, that or the other, but it is “not done” to say it… A genuinely unfashionable opinion is almost never given a fair hearing.’
The fake, earliest form (1982): ‘In a time of deceit, telling the truth is a revolutionary act.’
The fake, standard form: ‘universal’ inserted; also ‘during times of’ and ‘in an age of.’
context.pull: The Orwell Society keeps a list of things he never said. This is on it.
